question: Your video call keeps freezing, but only when someone in the kitchen warms up their lunch. Which appliance is jamming your Wi-Fi?
topic: Home Wi-Fi routers and dead zones
source_excerpt: A running microwave operates at 2.45 GHz and leaks a small amount of that energy past its shielding, swamping nearby 802.11b/g/n routers that share the band.

extra.why_interesting: Players blame the router or the internet provider for random dropouts and never suspect the kitchen. The idea that warming up leftovers can knock out a video call is a small revelation, and most players can reason their way to it.
extra.verification_notes: Microwave ovens operate at ~2.45 GHz, overlapping the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi band and disrupting it; no newer developments change this (https://www.scienceabc.com/innovation/do-microwaves-interfere-with-wifi-signals).

explanation: A microwave oven runs at about 2.45 gigahertz, right in the middle of the 2.4 gigahertz Wi-Fi band. The little energy that leaks out can drown out your router's much weaker signal. Switching your devices to the 5 gigahertz band usually avoids the problem.

question: A big hallway mirror can create a Wi-Fi dead zone behind it, even though plain glass lets the signal through. What is hiding in the mirror that blocks the Wi-Fi?
topic: Home Wi-Fi routers and dead zones
source_excerpt: the thin metal layer behind a mirror reflects radio signals as well as light

extra.why_interesting: People think of a mirror as just glass, and glass lets Wi-Fi through. The hidden metal layer that makes it reflect your face also reflects the radio signal, which turns an ordinary decoration into a Wi-Fi blocker.
extra.verification_notes: Mirrors have a thin metallic (silver/aluminum) backing that reflects Wi-Fi radio waves, so the claimed answer is correct; sources are consumer-tech pages, and no contradicting or newer information was found.

explanation: Every mirror has a very thin layer of metal behind the glass, usually silver or aluminium. The same layer that bounces light back to show your reflection also bounces the radio waves back toward the router.
